<meta>continues the list of the five elements of escape, following sections on renunciation, non-ill-will, and non-cruelty</meta>

5. Furthermore, monks, when a monk attends to <term>rūpa</term> <gloss>form</gloss>¹, his mind does not leap forward, does not gain confidence, does not settle down, and is not released into forms². However, when he attends to the <term>arūpa</term> <gloss>formless</gloss>, his mind leaps forward, gains confidence, settles down, and is released. His mind is well-directed, well-developed, well-risen, well-released, and well-detached from forms. Whatever <term>āsavā</term> <gloss>taints</gloss>, distress, or feverish anxieties might arise conditioned by form, he is free from them. He does not experience that feeling. This is declared to be the escape from forms.

6. Furthermore, monks, when a monk attends to <term>sakkāya</term> <gloss>identity or the view of a permanent self</gloss>, his mind does not leap forward, does not gain confidence, does not settle down, and is not released. However, when he attends to the <term>sakkāyanirodha</term> <gloss>cessation of identity</gloss>, his mind leaps forward, gains confidence, settles down, and is released. His mind is well-directed, well-developed, well-risen, well-released, and well-detached from identity. Whatever taints, distress, or feverish anxieties might arise conditioned by identity, he is free from them. He does not experience that feeling. This is declared to be the escape from identity.

For such a monk, <term>kāmanandi</term> <gloss>delight in sensual pleasure</gloss>³ no longer lies latent. <term>Vyāpādanandi</term> <gloss>delight in ill-will</gloss>³ no longer lies latent. <term>Vihesānandi</term> <gloss>delight in cruelty</gloss>⁴ no longer lies latent. <term>Rūpanandi</term> <gloss>delight in form</gloss>³ no longer lies latent. <term>Sakkāyanandi</term> <gloss>delight in identity</gloss>³ no longer lies latent. Because he is without latent tendencies⁵ toward delight in sensuality, ill-will, cruelty, form, and identity, this monk⁶ is called, monks, <term>niranusayo</term> <gloss>one without latent tendencies</gloss>⁷. He has cut off⁸ <term>taṇha</term> <gloss>craving</gloss>, discarded⁹ the <term>samyojana</term> <gloss>fetters</gloss>, and by the full understanding of conceit, he has made an end of <term>dukkhassa</term> <gloss>suffering</gloss>.

These, monks, are the five elements of escape¹⁰.

->The Brahmin Chapter¹¹, the Twentieth¹².<-

---

¹ <note>Siamese edition reads: in form</note>
² <note>Siamese edition reads: in forms</note>
³ <note>Thai edition reads: delight (with a long vowel)</note>
⁴ <note>Omitted by the Thai edition</note>
⁵ <note>Omitted by the Burmese manuscript M₆</note>
⁶ <note>Manuscripts M. and Ph. read: of the monk</note>
⁷ <note>Manuscript M. reads: without latent tendencies; M. and Ph. read: no latent tendencies; Siamese edition reads: without attachment</note>
⁸ <note>Thai edition and M₆ read: he cut off; the reading in manuscript M. is entirely corrupt</note>
⁹ <note>Thai, M₆, and M. read: he turned away; Ph. reads: he turned away</note>
¹⁰ <note>Thai edition reads: escape</note>
¹¹ <note>Thai, M₆, and M. read: The Great Chapter; the remaining text is missing in those versions; Ph. adds: finished</note>
¹² <note>Ph. reads: twentieth, though using the masculine form for chapter; omitted by M.; Siamese edition has: fifth; M., Ph., and Siamese editions insert before the Table of Contents: The Fourth Fifty [section of fifty discourses] is finished (Siamese edition adds: finished)</note>

<summary>This page concludes the discourse on the five elements of escape, focusing on the transition from form to the formless and from identity to the cessation of identity. A monk who masters these escapes is described as having eliminated all latent tendencies and ended suffering.</summary>
<keywords>Nissaraniya-dhatu, Rupa, Arupa, Sakkaya, Taints, Latent tendencies, Asava, Nirvana, Brahmin Chapter, Anguttara Nikaya</keywords>
